evidence: This is an argument against volume conduction as an explanation for the observed coherence.

claim: The observed coherence is non-homogenous among the different cerebellar lobules, in contrast to what one would expect if theta was volume conducted from a common location.
source: 3) By recording simultaneously from hippocampus and multiple cerebellar regions, we have been able to demonstrate that the observed coherence is non-homogenous among the different cerebellar lobules in contrast to what one would expect if theta was volume conducted from a common location.
evidence: This is an argument against volume conduction as an explanation for the observed coherence.

claim: Results obtained using the imaginary part of coherency, which is not influenced by volume conduction, were remarkably similar to those obtained using standard coherence analysis in the linear track paradigm.
source: 4) We calculated the imaginary part of coherency, which is not influenced by volume conduction (Nolte et al., 2004), in the linear track paradigm and found results that were remarkably similar to those obtained using standard coherence analysis.
evidence: This is an argument against volume conduction as an explanation for the observed coherence, supported by a citation.

claim: Purkinje cell spikes in lobule VI of the cerebellum can phase lock to hippocampal theta oscillations.
source: 5) We showed that Purkinje cell spikes in lobule VI of the cerebellum can phase lock to hippocampal theta oscillations.
evidence: This is an argument against volume conduction as an explanation for the observed coherence.

claim: Theta rhythms in the hippocampus preferentially synchronize with those in discrete regions of the cerebellum.
source: Importantly, we have shown for the first time that theta rhythms in the hippocampus preferentially synchronize with those in discrete regions of the cerebellum and that the degree of this coupling changes depending upon the behavioral context.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the physiological findings of the study.

claim: The degree of coupling between hippocampal and cerebellar theta rhythms changes depending upon the behavioral context.
source: Importantly, we have shown for the first time that theta rhythms in the hippocampus preferentially synchronize with those in discrete regions of the cerebellum and that the degree of this coupling changes depending upon the behavioral context.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the physiological findings of the study.

claim: Lobule VI-HPC coherence was dominant during active movement in the home-cage and remained stable during learning of the real world linear track task.
source: Lobule VI-HPC coherence was dominant during active movement in the home-cage and remained stable during learning of the real world linear track task.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the physiological findings of the study.

claim: Crus I - HPC coherence was highly dynamic, showing a significant increase over learning of the real world linear track task and becoming dominant after the acquisition of a goal-directed behavior.
source: On the other hand, Crus I - HPC coherence was highly dynamic, showing a significant increase over learning of the real world linear track task and becoming dominant after the acquisition of a goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the physiological findings of the study.

claim: High Crus I-HPC coherence was sustained across the linear track when the animal performed goal-directed behavior but not during the early training, exploratoration phase.
source: Furthermore, we reveal that high Crus I-HPC coherence was sustained across the linear track when the animal performed goal-directed behavior but not during the early training, exploratoration phase.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the physiological findings of the study.

claim: Sustained Crus I-HPC coherence may be related to the ability of the cerebellum, and particular Crus I, to link internal and external sensory context with specific action toward the goal.
source: Such sustained coherence may be related to the ability of the cerebellum, and particular Crus I, to link internal and external sensory context with specific action toward the goal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the physiological findings.

claim: A recent study has suggested that Purkinje cells in the Crus I region and neurons in its output, the dentate nucleus, exhibit firing rate modulation in anticipation of expected reward in a VR task.
source: In line with this hypothesis, a recent study has suggested that Purkinje cells in the Crus I region and neurons in its output, the dentate nucleus, exhibit firing rate modulation in anticipation of expected reward in a VR task (Chabrol et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The activity of Purkinje cells in lateral Crus I was modulated by running and/or visual flow speed.
source: Interestingly, they show that the activity of Purkinje cells in lateral Crus I was modulated by running and/or visual flow speed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Crus I-HPC coherence remained present when animals performed goal-modulated behavior in VR, although multiple streams of sensory input, such as vestibular, whisker and olfactory, become irrelevant and even confounding in the head-restricted virtual environment task.
source: This is consistent with our examples showing that Crus I-HPC coherence remained present when animals performed goal-modulated behavior in VR, although multiple streams of sensory input, such as vestibular, whisker and olfactory, become irrelevant and even confounding in the head-restricted virtual environment task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the physiological findings in the virtual reality task.

claim: Within lobule VI, the A module receives multi-modal sensory information, mainly arising from collicular and vestibular centers.
source: Within lobule VI, the A module receives multi-modal sensory information, mainly arising from collicular and vestibular centers (Voogd and Barmack, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The superior colliculus plays a role in visual processing and generation of orienting behaviors.
source: The superior colliculus plays a role in visual processing and generation of orienting behaviors (Basso and May, 2017), which might be relevant for the establishment and maintenance of the hippocampal spatial map, and thus may be required constantly during active movement, independent of the specific behavioral task.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The persistent and similar levels of lobule VI-HPC coherence during active movement in the homecage and linear track task, in both real world and virtual reality environment tasks is in agreement with the hypothesis that the A module's multi-modal sensory input is relevant for the establishment and maintenance of the hippocampal spatial map.
source: The persistent and similar levels of lobule VI-HPC coherence during active movement in the homecage and linear track task, in both real world and virtual reality environment tasks is in agreement with such a hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the physiological findings and the known functions of the A module.

claim: In monkeys and humans, Crus I is anatomically and functionally associated with prefrontal cortex.
source: In monkeys and humans, Crus I is anatomically and functionally associated with prefrontal cortex (Kelly and Strick, 2003; Iglói et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In mouse Crus I, the D2 module receives convergent sensory and motor information.
source: In mouse Crus I, the D2 module receives convergent sensory and motor information (Proville et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The D2 module has been found to contain internal models, a neural representation of one's body and the external world based on memory of previous experiences, that are used for visuo-motor coordination.
source: Furthermore, this module has been found to contain internal models, a neural representation of one's body and the external world based on memory of previous experiences, that are used for visuo-motor coordination (Cerminara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

source: Similarly, the C2 module has been found to also participate in visuo-motor processing related to limb coordination during goal-directed reaching (Cerminara and Apps, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

source: Both modules might be particularly important during the acquisition of a goal-directed behavior such as our real-world linear track task in which animals needed to reach non-cued reward zones.

source: Our finding that Crus I-HPC coherence increases during task learning fits with this hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the physiological findings and the known functions of these modules.

source: In summary, our results suggest the existence of anatomically discrete hippocampal-cerebellar network interactions with a prominent involvement of Crus I during goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

source: Both anatomical and electrophysiological data point toward involvement of the theta generating pathway in cerebellum-hippocampus interactions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.
